body.en: Calculus rests on a single idea: what value does a function approach as its input creeps toward a target? It need not ever reach that value — what matters is the trend.
We write \( \displaystyle \lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \) if the outputs \( f(x) \) can be made as close to \( L \) as we like by taking \( x \) sufficiently close to \( c \) (but not equal to \( c \)).

The function may even be undefined exactly at \( c \). Consider \( \displaystyle f(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x-1} \). At \( x=1 \) the formula gives \( \tfrac{0}{0} \), yet factoring reveals \( f(x)=x+1 \) everywhere else, so the curve heads straight for \( 2 \).

body.en:
Sometimes the approach differs by direction. The left-hand limit \( \displaystyle \lim_{x\to c^-} f(x) \) and right-hand limit \( \displaystyle \lim_{x\to c^+} f(x) \) must agree for the two-sided limit to exist:

\[ \lim_{x\to c} f(x)=L \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \lim_{x\to c^-}f(x)=\lim_{x\to c^+}f(x)=L. \]

A function \( f \) is continuous at \( c \) when all three hold: (i) \( f(c) \) is defined, (ii) \( \displaystyle\lim_{x\to c} f(x) \) exists, and (iii) the two are equal, \( \displaystyle\lim_{x\to c} f(x)=f(c) \). Informally: you can draw it through \( c \) without lifting the pen.

label.en: ● Complete Taxonomy of Graphs of Continuity & Discontinuity

body.en:
A function \(f\) is classified at a point \(x = c\) by rigorously evaluating the Three-Part Continuity Checklist:

  1. Condition 1: \(f(c)\) is defined (the point \(c\) lies in the domain of \(f\)).
  2. Condition 2: The two-sided limit \(\lim_{x\to c} f(x)\) exists (meaning \(\lim_{x\to c^-} f(x) = \lim_{x\to c^+} f(x) = L\), both finite).
  3. Condition 3: The limit equals the function value: \(\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = f(c)\).

Depending on which conditions hold or fail, graphs exhibit one of six fundamental geometric cases:

  • Case 1 · Continuous everywhere at \(c\): All 3 conditions pass. The graph is unbroken at \(x = c\).
  • Case 2 · Removable Discontinuity (Hole): Condition 1 fails (\(f(c)\) is undefined), but Condition 2 passes (\(\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L\) exists). The graph displays an open circle at \((c, L)\).
  • Case 3 · Removable Discontinuity (Displaced Point): Conditions 1 & 2 pass, but Condition 3 fails (\(\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L \neq f(c)\)). The graph features an open circle at \((c, L)\) and an isolated solid dot at \((c, f(c))\).
  • Case 4 · Jump Discontinuity: Condition 2 fails because one-sided limits are finite but unequal: \(\lim_{x\to c^-} f(x) \neq \lim_{x\to c^+} f(x)\). The graph abruptly jumps between two different heights.
  • Case 5 · Infinite Discontinuity (Vertical Asymptote): Condition 2 fails because at least one one-sided limit is \(+\infty\) or \(-\infty\). The graph shoots vertically alongside the line \(x = c\).
  • Case 6 · Essential / Oscillating Discontinuity: Condition 2 fails because outputs oscillate infinitely many times between bounds as \(x \to c\) (e.g. \(f(x) = \sin(2/(x-c))\)). No single finite limit exists.

label.en: ● Definition 1.3 — Precise (ε, δ) Definition of Limit

body.en:
Let \(f\) be a function defined on an open interval containing \(c\), except possibly at \(c\) itself. We write:

\[ \lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \]

if and only if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a \(\delta > 0\) such that:

\[ 0 < |x - c| < \delta \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon. \]

Geometric Meaning: No matter how narrow a target horizontal corridor \((L - \varepsilon, L + \varepsilon)\) is specified around \(L\), there is a corresponding input tolerance window \((c - \delta, c + \delta)\) around \(c\) such that every point on the graph within that window (excluding \(x = c\)) is trapped strictly inside the target corridor.

label.en: Rigorous ε-δ Proofs — Linear and Quadratic Functions

body.en:
Example 1 (Linear Limit): Prove using the \(\varepsilon\text{--}\delta\) definition that \(\lim_{x\to 3} (4x - 5) = 7\).

1. Scratchwork (Discovery): We need \(|(4x - 5) - 7| < \varepsilon\). Simplifying gives \(|4x - 12| = 4|x - 3| < \varepsilon \iff |x - 3| < \frac{\varepsilon}{4}\). This reveals our choice: \(\delta = \frac{\varepsilon}{4}\).

2. Formal Deductive Proof: Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) be given arbitrary. Choose \(\delta = \frac{\varepsilon}{4}\). Since \(\varepsilon > 0\), \(\delta > 0\). Assume \(0 < |x - 3| < \delta\). Then: \[ |(4x - 5) - 7| = |4x - 12| = 4|x - 3| < 4\delta = 4\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\right) = \varepsilon. \] Thus, by the \(\varepsilon\text{--}\delta\) definition, \(\lim_{x\to 3}(4x - 5) = 7\). \(\blacksquare\)

Example 2 (Quadratic Limit with Bounding): Prove that \(\lim_{x\to 2} x^2 = 4\).

1. Scratchwork: We want \(|x^2 - 4| < \varepsilon\). Factoring: \(|x^2 - 4| = |x - 2| \cdot |x + 2|\). We must bound the extraneous factor \(|x + 2|\). Establish a preliminary constraint \(\delta \le 1\). Then \(|x - 2| < 1 \implies 1 < x < 3 \implies 3 < x + 2 < 5 \implies |x + 2| < 5\). Therefore: \[ |x^2 - 4| = |x - 2| \cdot |x + 2| < 5|x - 2|. \] To ensure this is \(< \varepsilon\), we require \(|x - 2| < \frac{\varepsilon}{5}\). Hence we choose \(\delta = \min\left(1, \frac{\varepsilon}{5}\right)\).

2. Formal Deductive Proof: Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) be arbitrary. Set \(\delta = \min\left(1, \frac{\varepsilon}{5}\right)\). Suppose \(0 < |x - 2| < \delta\). Because \(\delta \le 1\), we have \(|x - 2| < 1 \implies |x + 2| < 5\). Because \(\delta \le \frac{\varepsilon}{5}\), we have \(|x - 2| < \frac{\varepsilon}{5}\). Consequently: \[ |x^2 - 4| = |x - 2| \cdot |x + 2| < \left(\frac{\varepsilon}{5}\right)(5) = \varepsilon. \] This completes the proof that \(\lim_{x\to 2} x^2 = 4\). \(\blacksquare\)

label.en: ● Precise Definitions of Limits at Infinity & Infinite Limits (with Proofs)

body.en:
1. Limit at Infinity: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to \infty} f(x) = L\) means that for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(M > 0\) such that \(x > M \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon\).

Proof: Prove that \(\lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{2x+1}{x+3} = 2\). Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) be given. We find \(\left|\frac{2x+1}{x+3} - 2\right| = \left|\frac{2x+1 - 2x - 6}{x+3}\right| = \frac{5}{x+3}\) for \(x > 0\). Setting \(\frac{5}{x+3} < \varepsilon \iff x+3 > \frac{5}{\varepsilon} \iff x > \frac{5}{\varepsilon} - 3\). Choose \(M = \max\left(1, \frac{5}{\varepsilon} - 3\right)\). For any \(x > M\): \[ \left|\frac{2x+1}{x+3} - 2\right| = \frac{5}{x+3} < \frac{5}{M+3} \le \frac{5}{(5/\varepsilon)} = \varepsilon. \quad \blacksquare \]

2. Infinite Limit at a Point: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = \infty\) means that for every \(M > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that \(0 < |x - c| < \delta \implies f(x) > M\).

Proof: Prove that \(\lim_{x\to 0} \frac{1}{x^2} = \infty\). Let \(M > 0\) be given arbitrary. Choose \(\delta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{M}} > 0\). Assume \(0 < |x - 0| < \delta\). Then \(|x| < \frac{1}{\sqrt{M}} \implies x^2 < \frac{1}{M}\). Taking reciprocals gives: \[ \frac{1}{x^2} > M. \quad \blacksquare \]

Evaluate \( \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 3}\frac{x^2-9}{x-3} \).

Direct substitution gives \( \tfrac00 \), so factor the numerator: \( x^2-9=(x-3)(x+3) \). Cancel the common factor (valid since \( x\neq 3 \) in the limit):

\[ \lim_{x\to 3}\frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{x-3}=\lim_{x\to 3}(x+3)=6. \]

caption.en: Plot of rational function \(f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3}\) showing a removable discontinuity (hole) at \((3, 6)\).

body.en:
Indeterminate Form 0/0: Obtaining \(\frac{0}{0}\) from direct substitution does NOT mean the limit is 0, 1, or does not exist. It is an indeterminate form signaling that an algebraic simplification (factoring, conjugate rationalization, trig identity, or L'Hôpital's Rule) must be performed.

Two-Sided Limit Existence: The overall limit \(\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L\) exists IF AND ONLY IF both one-sided limits exist and agree: \(\lim_{x\to c^-} f(x) = \lim_{x\to c^+} f(x) = L\). For piece-wise and absolute value functions, always verify both directions separately.

Continuity Checklist: A function \(f\) is continuous at \(x = c\) only if all 3 conditions hold: (1) \(f(c)\) is defined; (2) \(\lim_{x\to c} f(x)\) exists; (3) \(\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = f(c)\).

solution.en: When \(x\) approaches 2 from the left (\(x < 2\)), \(x - 2 < 0\), so \(|x - 2| = -(x - 2)\). Substituting gives \(\lim_{x\to 2^-} \frac{-(x - 2)}{x - 2} = \lim_{x\to 2^-} (-1) = -1\). (Note: from the right, the limit is \(+1\), so the two-sided limit does not exist).
